transcript:
[00:00] Aisha (Redwood): All right everyone, thanks for joining. we got 35 minutes today. quick roll call?
[00:07] Liam (Skyline): hey, Liam here.
[00:09] Priya (Skyline): Priya here.
[00:11] Carlos (Skyline): Carlos, on SRE.
[00:13] Nora (Skyline): Nora, product.
[00:15] Marco (Redwood): Marco, SE.
[00:17] Jenna (Redwood): Jenna, CSM.
[00:19] Aisha: Cool. quick status: you ran the integration tests last week — Priya, can you summarize surface-level results?
[00:29] Priya: yeah so we wired the SDK into our orchestration — mostly the node SDK — and we hit a couple things. Structured output is coming back but there's munging on the entities array, sometimes the tool metadata ends up as a string instead of an object. also we saw request latencies at P95 around 520ms in the dev env, with spikes to 900 when we batch bigger.
[00:48] Marco: ok that aligns with what we expected; looks like a schema mismatch between your parser and the SDK helper's default function call encoding. we recently shipped a fix that adds explicit content-type and an example usage with structured output; i'll share that snippet.
[01:05] Priya: sweet, is that the one you pushed to the repo last week? i looked but i wasn't sure it was the canonical snippet.
[01:12] Marco: yeah there are two copies, sorry. canonical one is in the integration-examples branch — link in the notes — it forces decode: true and sets output_schema to the model helper. that should make the entities come back as arrays of objects rather than a stringified blob.
[01:28] Aisha: i'll follow up and put the exact file in the slack thread.
[01:31] Liam: i also noticed some tokenization differences — the summary prompt sometimes truncates bullet points. is that a model param we can tune?
[01:40] Marco: yes, that's mostly temperature/top_p/stop tokens and the max_tokens cutoff. for structured outputs we usually recommend lower temperature, top_p 0.95, and explicit stop sequences. also use deterministic sampling when you need exact schemas — set temperature to 0.
[01:55] Nora: can you explain deterministic sampling vs the sampling you use by default?
[01:58] Marco: sure — default generation uses stochastic sampling for variety which can cause small schema drift, so deterministic is temperature 0, greedy or beam-like behavior; it keeps structure stable. it's a tradeoff with creative outputs.
[02:15] Priya: got it. next, the SDK function calls — we attempted to do tool calling where the model returns a function name and args, then our runtime executes it. some of the function payloads were nested and our runner choked on unexpected keys.
[02:29] Marco: we can add a small adapter in the SDK that flattens known tool args and validates shape. i'll send a minimal adapter you can drop into your runner. could you paste one example of the payload that failed?
[02:40] Priya: yeah here's one i pasted in the doc — the tool name was 'search_documents' but the args came as a single string: '{"query":"invoice"}' instead of a JSON object.
[02:50] Marco: hm, that's the same symptom as the structured output mis-parse; likely an encoding/serialization mismatch where the model helper wraps args in a string to avoid tokenization errors. i can change the helper to emit args as native JSON when we set function_mode: strict.
[03:05] Aisha: this is a good place to mention that for the POC we recommended using Redwood-hosted dev endpoints to keep network complexity low; once you're happy we'll exercise Dedicated/VPC. any blockers to continuing on hosted for the next run?
[03:18] Carlos: our security team prefers running initial runs on hosted but with IP allowlist and retention controls — do you have short-term retention policy options?
[03:27] Jenna: yes we expose a retention setting per-project; for pilots we can set to 7 days, and we also offer opt-out and private deployment options if you need stricter controls. i'll attach the retention doc.
[03:40] Carlos: also need a network diagram for our security review. we heard mention of VPC peering for private later — what's the typical pattern?
[03:48] Marco: typical is to start on hosted for iteration, then for Dedicated we provision a customer VPC with peering and route traffic to dedicated GPU pools. for private on-prem we ship an appliance. i'll add a short network diagram and the IP ranges.
[04:02] Liam: perfect. on performance: the P95 520ms — is that with batching enabled?
[04:09] Marco: yes that's with a batch window of 20ms and dynamic batching turned on. if you reduce batch window you'll see lower tail latency at cost of less batching efficiency. we can tune batch size and batching timeout per route.
[04:22] Priya: what's the unit cost tradeoff? we need to quantify tokens per second vs latency.
[04:27] Aisha: we'll share a small spreadsheet mapping batch window to cost delta using your expected qps; i'll include an example using your 200 qps baseline.
[04:35] Nora: about quantization — we discussed 4-bit vs 8-bit models last week; any recs for production relevance vs cost?
[04:42] Marco: yes, for retrieval/short-answer workloads 4-bit quantized models tend to be fine and give huge cost wins; for higher-fidelity structured generation we recommend 8-bit or mixed precision to reduce hallucination risk. Redwood Optimize has suggestion profiles — i'll attach recommended profiles for your workload.
[04:59] Priya: thanks. another small thing: the SDK's error payloads were sometimes 500 with no body, making retries hard. can we get a clearer error shape?
[05:07] Marco: agreed, we rolled out structured error bodies in the latest SDK; make sure you're on v1.3.2. also we added a request-id header so you can correlate logs.
[05:16] Carlos: good — that's vital. please confirm header name?
[05:19] Marco: X-Redwood-Request-Id.
[05:21] Priya: noted.
[05:23] Aisha: quick sync on function/tool calling flow — the recommended pattern is: 1) model suggests function call + args, 2) SDK validates + normalizes args, 3) runtime executes tool, 4) model ingests tool result as a structured object and continues. any deviations from that?
[05:36] Marco: that's the canonical pattern. for your runner you might want step 2 to also include schema validation against a JSON Schema. we can generate a schema from the function signature automatically.
[05:46] Nora: could that schema be included in the SDK helper?
[05:49] Marco: yes, we'll generate and include it in the snippet.
[05:52] Liam: one operational concern — we have bursts up to 800 qps for short 30s windows. how does Redwood handle that with Dedicated vs Hosted?
[06:02] Marco: on Hosted we have autoscaling & burst pools but there can be cold-penalty; Dedicated gives you reserved GPU capacity and predictable throughput. for spikes we recommend reserved baseline plus burst configuration; we can model cost for both.
[06:17] Aisha: we'll run a cost model for your burst pattern and share.
[06:21] Priya: re: schema, i want the structured output to always include a top-level 'entities' array and 'confidence' per entity — can we gate that?
[06:31] Marco: yes set output_schema to require entities[*].confidence and entities[*].type. we can also add a post-processor in SDK to reject responses that fail schema.
[06:41] Priya: what about partial outputs? sometimes the model returns partial results mid-stream; our consumer expects full JSON only.
[06:48] Marco: for streaming you can buffer until you detect the final token or use a stream delimiter. we added a streaming mode in the SDK that emits full object only on completion when you set stream_mode: complete.
[06:59] Nora: this streaming buffer — does it add latency?
[07:02] Marco: minimal, it buffers only until finalization; if you need microsecond-level latency you should avoid complete buffering and handle incremental deltas.
[07:12] Priya: okay we'll try stream_mode: complete for our app.
[07:15] Aisha: quick security check: SSO / SAML for your org — are you planning to have multiple stakeholders with RBAC?
[07:23] Liam: yes, we need SSO + role-based access. also audit logs retention to 90 days ideally.
[07:29] Jenna: we support SAML SSO and granular RBAC. audit logs can be exported to your SIEM; default retention is 90 days on enterprise tier. i'll include the export doc.
[07:40] Carlos: will we get per-token cost visibility? our finance team needs line items.
[07:44] Aisha: yes Console provides token-level cost and per-route breakdowns; we can also send daily CSV exports to an S3 bucket.
[07:53] Priya: nice. next, small debugging note — we saw occasional 'kv cache not found' errors in the runtime when we resumed sessions after a pause. any idea?
[08:02] Marco: that sounds like the ephemeral KV eviction on lower-tier runs; if you pin sessions with session_persistence: true it stores KV longer, or use our hosted session store. we'll check logs.
[08:13] Aisha: please attach one example log snippet so Marco can triage.
[08:18] Priya: will do.
[08:20] Nora: timeline question — if POC goes well, when can we graduate to a Dedicated pilot?
[08:24] Aisha: typically 4-6 weeks after initial integration; depends on procurement and network reviews. we can parallelize some tasks like compliance review to shorten that.
[08:33] Liam: procurement will need a pilot contract and SLAs. can you share a sample?
[08:37] Jenna: yes i'll send a pilot MSA and SLA template after this call.
[08:41] Priya: small UX ask — the SDK's structured output debug mode currently logs raw tokens which are noisy; can we add a pretty-print debug mode?
[08:50] Marco: absolutely, we'll add a debug.print_structured option that pretty prints and validates.
[08:55] Aisha: great. let's summarize next steps — i'll read them out. Marco will share SDK snippet + adapter + schema generator by Friday the 12th, Jenna will share SOC2 and pilot MSA and retention docs by Monday the 14th, Priya/Carlos will run the 1k request smoke test and share logs by the 17th, and we'll schedule a dedicated latency/cost benchmark wk of 22nd. any changes?
[09:18] Priya: no that's correct.
[09:20] Liam: sounds good.
[09:22] Nora: thanks everyone.
[09:24] Aisha: ok thanks all, we'll follow up in the thread with links. end call.
[09:29] <meeting ends>
